notes:
I found plenty of traditional commentary on all nine verses. I didn't find real disagreements between Protestant traditions, and I found nothing from the modern-scholarship sites (bibleodyssey.org, netbible.org) or on prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace teaching. Those parts are left out, as you asked. The only Catholic/Orthodox source I reached was Augustine on newadvent.org. Pulpit, Ellicott, Calvin, Clarke and others are quoted through biblehub/studylight pages, not their own sources.

**The psalm as a whole**
- Gill says this psalm starts the "Hallel" (Psalms 113–118), sung at Jewish feasts. Some think it was the hymn Christ and his apostles sang after the Lord's Supper. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/113.htm
- Guzik says the opening verses about God's greatness prepare for the reversal at the end, where the most powerful being lifts the lowly from the dust and ash heap to sit with princes. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-113/
- Preceptaustin quotes the view that the psalm links the Song of Hannah and the Magnificat of the Virgin. https://www.preceptaustin.org/psalm_113_commentary

**v. 1**
- In Gill's view, "servants of the LORD" means all the saints, a holy priesthood, not just angels or priests and Levites. "The name" means God himself and his perfections. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/113.htm
- Gill notes that some see the threefold repetition as pointing to the Trinity, but he thinks this is doubtful and not enough to build a doctrine on. Spurgeon is more open to it, calling it a thinly veiled allusion to that holy mystery. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/113-1.htm
- Poole includes the Levites, who were specially devoted to this work, along with all faithful people. The Pulpit Commentary says faithful Israelites are certainly meant, but the phrase need not be limited to them. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/113-1.htm
- Guzik explains praising the name as honouring Yahweh himself and his character. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-113/
- **Catholic (Augustine):** His Latin text reads "Praise the Lord, you children." Augustine applies this to all ages, since Paul tells believers to be children in malice, and he names pride as the malice in question. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801113.htm

**v. 2**
- Gill: to "bless" the name means to honour and glorify it. He reads "from this time" as the time of writing, the time of a believer's conversion, or the whole Gospel age. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/113.htm
- Guzik: the unchanging God never stops deserving praise. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-113/
- **Augustine:** "From this" means from the moment ye speak these words. He adds that only the humble ("children") can praise, because the proud do not know how. https://www.ccel.org/ccel/schaff/npnf108.ii.CXIII.html

**v. 3**
- Gill says the phrase is about place, not time: all the lands from east to west. He links it to Malachi 1:11 and the Gospel going to all nations. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/113.htm
- Guzik reads it as Hebrew repetition stressing *continual* praise. Note the contrast: Gill makes it about place, Guzik about time. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-113/
- Benson: all nations should praise God because they all benefit from creation and providence. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/113-1.htm
- **Augustine:** the verse speaks of wherever the Church has spread. https://www.ccel.org/ccel/schaff/npnf108.ii.CXIII.html

**v. 4**
- Gill: God's glory goes beyond what the heavens can declare. He applies this to Christ ascended above the heavens (Hebrews 1:4). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/113.htm
- Guzik: the covenant God of little Israel is greater than everything in creation. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-113/

**v. 5**
- Gill: no one compares with God, whether the gods of the nations, the angels or earthly kings. He notes the alternative reading "who exalteth himself to dwell." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/113.htm
- Barnes: the Hebrew literally means "The one making high to sit", the picture of a lofty throne. Pulpit: even the highest creature is immeasurably far from God. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/113-5.htm

**v. 6**
- Pulpit: it is condescension for God even to look at heaven (Job 15:15), and much more so to look at earth. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/113-6.htm
- Guzik links this to Psalm 8:4. He quotes Maclaren: God's loftiness and his condescension each have to be measured by the other. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-113/
- Gill applies the verse to Christ, who humbled himself to come to earth and die on the cross. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/113.htm
- Henry makes a similar point about the Son of God coming to seek the lost. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/113-5.htm

**v. 7**
- Cambridge Bible: verses 7–8 are taken almost word for word from Hannah's song (1 Samuel 2:8). Sitting in the dust or on the dunghill is an Eastern image for deep misery. The dunghill was the town rubbish heap, and Ellicott adds that tradition says Job sat on one. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/113-7.htm
- Barnes: this is not a universal truth that it always happens, but one of the works that show God's power and goodness. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/113-7.htm
- Gill reads it two ways. Literally, God raised humble people like Saul and David. Spiritually, he lifts sinners from the "dust of sin." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/113.htm
- Benson: one rabbi applied the verse to the resurrection, and Christian writers to redemption in Christ. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/113-7.htm
- Guzik suggests that when Jesus sang this on the night of his arrest, he may have seen himself as the one to be raised from the dust of the grave. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-113/

**v. 8**
- Guzik connects the verse to Ephesians 2:5–6, believers seated with Christ in heavenly places. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-113/
- Pulpit gives historical examples: Joseph, Saul, David, Daniel and Mordecai. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/113-8.htm
- Gill: "princes of his people" means the patriarchs, prophets and apostles the saints will sit with in heaven. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/113.htm
- Text note (Cambridge): with the Greek Old Testament, the reading should almost certainly be "to set him" instead of the standard Hebrew form. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/113-8.htm

**v. 9**
- Ellicott: only motherhood gave a wife a secure place in her husband's house. The verse alludes to Hannah, and he also takes the mother as a picture of the nation restored. https://biblehub.com/psalms/113-9.htm
- Calvin: the Hebrew word means "household," not just "house," so the point is a home filled with children. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/113-9.html
- Spurgeon lists Sarah, Rachel, Manoah's wife, Hannah and Elizabeth as literal fulfilments. He also applies the verse to spiritual barrenness, as comfort for those who have never won souls. https://www.preceptaustin.org/psalm_113_commentary
- Readings differ on who the "barren woman" is:
  - Clarke: the captives in Babylon and their return. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/113-9.html
  - Pulpit: Israel is the true barren woman (Isaiah 54:1). https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-113.html
  - Gill: the Church growing with converts, noting the Targum reads it of Israel's congregation. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/113.htm
- Bible.org (Deffinbaugh): the psalm ends with one barren woman to show God cares for the individual, not just needy people in general. https://bible.org/seriespage/psalm-113-god-great-and-he-gracious
- **Augustine:** he reads it of the Church and Abraham's seed, like the stars of heaven and the sand of the sea. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801113.htm
